CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and inflammation → Recruitment and polarization of TAMs with high TGF-β signaling → Establishment of an immunosuppressive TME impairing effector T-cell function → Targeted delivery of high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 via dual-targeting nanoparticles to disrupt TGF-β receptors in TAMs → Reprogramming TAMs from an M2 (immunosuppressive) to an M1 (pro-inflammatory) phenotype → Enhanced antigen presentation and effector T-cell activation → Improved efficacy of conventional immunotherapies in HCC
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a refined therapeutic strategy employing dual-targeting nanoparticles to deliver high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 systems specifically to tumor-associated macrophages in HCC can effectively disrupt TGF-β receptor (TGF-βR) signaling. This targeted disruption is expected to reprogram TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype. The consequent enhancement in antigen presentation and T-cell activation will synergize with conventional immunotherapies to achieve superior antitumor responses. Specifically, by incorporating advanced ligand-directed nanoparticle design, rigorous safety switches to prevent off-target gene editing, and detailed preclinical monitoring protocols, this approach addresses previous translational limitations while preserving the original causal chain of chronic liver injury-induced TAM polarization leading to an immunosuppressive TME.
Abstract: We propose an advanced therapeutic strategy to overcome the immunosuppressive microenvironment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by integrating precise CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing with state-of-the-art nanoparticle delivery systems. Specifically, our approach involves the targeted disruption of TGF-β receptor signaling in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), using dual-targeting nanoparticles designed to selectively deliver high‐fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 constructs to cells within the tumor and hepatic environment. This intervention aims to reprogram TAMs from an M2, immunosuppressive phenotype to an M1, pro-inflammatory state, thereby enhancing antigen presentation and effector T-cell activation. This reprogramming is anticipated to create a more permissive tumor microenvironment (TME) that can synergize with conventional immunotherapies, such as checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-T cells, to improve overall antitumor efficacy. We also detail refined targeting mechanisms, safety switches, and off-target monitoring strategies to address previous technical challenges.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis builds directly on the original concept by preserving its critical causal chain (chronic liver injury → TAM polarization → immunosuppressive TME → targeted CRISPR/Cas9 delivery → TAM reprogramming → enhanced immunotherapy synergy). Key enhancements include: (1) using dual-targeting nanoparticles that not only focus on hepatocytes/tumor cells but are further optimized for specificity to TAMs; (2) incorporating high-fidelity CRISPR/Cas9 systems accompanied by safety switches and rigorous off-target analysis; and (3) providing detailed mechanistic insights and preclinical experimental validation plans. These modifications improve the practical implementability of the strategy using contemporary technological capabilities while retaining logical coherence and novelty.
